$comment: The "what can go wrong" cases of the Failures simulation. Every outcome rests on the specification: bundle processing (Channel state transitions §2 and §6), replies and response ordering (Messaging §5, §7 and §8), slashing (Stakes and bonds §2, a Recommendation), the recovery table (CLPR Service §7) or the trust model (Overview §4). The first ref is the passage the simulation shows as the source; recovery names the row of the CLPR Service §7 recovery table a case follows.

cases.q: The application on the other side fails
cases.what: The bundle still succeeds. The reply carries APPLICATION_ERROR, and the other messages in the bundle are processed normally. Delivery worked; the application did not accept the message.
cases.pays: Under the recommended design the connector pays the execution charge, as for any delivered message, and is not slashed, because the failure is not its fault. On EVM ledgers it is slashed if that charge itself fails after dispatch.
cases.recovers: Nothing to recover. The sending application decides what to do with the error.

cases.q: The connector was never registered on the other side
cases.what: The message gets a deterministic answer: CONNECTOR_NOT_FOUND. The application is not called.
cases.pays: Under the recommended slashing rules, nobody is slashed on the destination, because there is no connector there; the submitter absorbs the execution cost. When the reply reaches the source, the source connector that authorized the message is slashed, and the penalty goes to the submitter of the bundle that carried the reply.
cases.recovers: Yes; the other messages in the same bundle are unaffected.

cases.q: The connector on the other side cannot pay
cases.what: CONNECTOR_UNDERFUNDED. The message is not dispatched and the failure reply is queued. Under the recommended slashing rules, the destination connector is slashed.
cases.pays: The penalty goes to the submitter of the bundle on the destination. The source connector is slashed too when the reply arrives. Penalties escalate, and repeated slashes end in a ban from the channel.
cases.recovers: Yes, once the connector can pay again, or the application uses another connector.

cases.q: An endpoint changes a message in transit
cases.what: Recomputing the running hash over the delivered messages no longer reproduces the proven running hash of the bundle's last message. The whole bundle is rejected before any message is dispatched.
cases.pays: The submitter paid its transaction fee and gets nothing back.
cases.state: ACTIVE (a rejected bundle changes no state)
cases.recovers: Immediately: any honest endpoint can deliver the genuine bundle.

cases.q: An endpoint re-submits an old bundle
cases.what: Messages the channel has already received are skipped, and every bundle must make progress: new messages, a trust anchor change, a newer endpoint manifest, a new acknowledgement or a step towards closing. An old bundle offers none of these, so it is rejected even if its proof is valid.
cases.pays: The submitter wasted its own transaction fee.

cases.q: All the endpoints on one side go offline
cases.what: Nothing is delivered. Messages queue up until the outbound queue reaches its depth limit, then new sends are refused. Nothing is lost or forged.
cases.recovers: Automatically, as soon as any endpoint, or anyone else, submits a valid bundle. Safety never depended on the endpoints; only liveness does.

cases.q: The other ledger goes down entirely
cases.what: Same as above from this side's point of view: the queue fills to its limit and then refuses new messages.
cases.recovers: When the peer is reachable again, sync resumes; message ids and running hashes keep delivery exact.

cases.q: Replies come back in the wrong order
cases.what: This is the only failure that changes a channel's status: it shows that the peer's outbound queue is inconsistent, which resending cannot repair. The channel is set to PAUSED: no new sends, and no message of a bundle with out-of-order replies is processed. Queued messages keep syncing to the peer.
cases.recovers: Automatically, once the peer's replies are in order: the first bundle accepted without a violation returns the channel to ACTIVE. Otherwise the administrator can close the channel; it drains once the peer is fixed. Messages that never get a reply are reconciled outside the protocol.

cases.q: The message is larger than the other side accepts
cases.what: Rejected at send time on the source ledger, against the limit the peer published, before it costs anyone a delivery. The destination independently rejects a bundle that exceeds its own limits.
cases.pays: The sender pays only the transaction fee of the failed send.

cases.q: Every endpoint on the other side was replaced and nobody knows the new addresses
cases.what: The list of peer endpoints is proven state. Anyone can obtain from the peer ledger a bundle that carries its current endpoint manifest and submit it as an ordinary transaction; the channel's copy is replaced and sync resumes. No connection to the old endpoints is needed.
cases.pays: Whoever submits pays a transaction fee.
cases.recovers: Yes; sync resumes with the new endpoints.

cases.q: The verifier turns out to be buggy or compromised
cases.what: The CLPR Service's own checks of message ids, running hash and reply order catch verifier bugs, not a compromised verifier, which can accept fabricated proofs. The administrator closes the channel; because a channel's verifier is fixed for its life, a new channel with a correct verifier is registered.
cases.pays: Whoever relied on the channel. Connector operators vet the verifier before staking on a channel.
cases.state: CLOSING (it drains and closes only if the peer's replies still arrive in order)
cases.recovers: Yes, on a new channel. Messages in flight when it closed can be lost and need reconciling outside the protocol.

cases.q: A ledger changes how its proofs look
cases.what: The channel's verifier can no longer check the new proofs, and a channel's verifier cannot be replaced. A new channel is registered with a new verifier, applications migrate, and the administrator closes the old channel.

cases.q: A ledger's own validators are compromised
cases.what: Then messages from that ledger can be forged, and CLPR does not claim otherwise. A message is no more trustworthy than the consensus that sealed it.
cases.pays: Everyone relying on that ledger, on-chain or cross-chain.
cases.recovers: Outside the protocol's scope. Beyond the two ledgers' consensus, the parts trusted are each ledger's CLPR Service, the channel's verifier and the remote application; endpoints and connectors cannot forge a message.
